Integral action responds to accumulated error and can remove steady-state error. Derivative action responds to how quickly error changes and can reduce overshoot when measurements are sufficiently clean.

For a sampled spreadsheet or simulator:

$$u_k=K_Pe_k+K_I\sum_{j=0}^{k}e_j\Delta t+K_D\frac{e_k-e_{k-1}}{\Delta t}$$

This finite-difference form does not require calculus.

| Mode | Benefit | Limitation |
|:--|:--|:--|
| P | fast, simple correction | steady-state error can remain |
| PI | removes persistent error | windup and added overshoot |
| PD | anticipates rapid change | noise sensitivity |
| PID | combines all actions | added tuning and protection |

Integral windup occurs when error keeps accumulating while the output is saturated. Limit or pause the accumulation as part of the simulation.

## Manual tuning sequence

1. Begin with every gain at zero.
2. Increase $K_P$ until the response is useful.
3. Add a small $K_I$ to remove remaining error.
4. Add $K_D$ only when the data quality supports it.
5. Compare graphs after every change.

[Download the required PID comparison activity](https://mrandrewandrade.github.io/assets/C06_Control_Methods_Comparison_Student.pdf). A physical PID build is optional.
